qs.q: Suppose that $A$ and $B$ are two matrices such that $AB=BA$. Then ----
e: Let $A$ be $m\times n$ and $B$ be $p\times q$.
$AB$ defined requires $n=p$; $BA$ defined requires $q=m$. So $B$ is $n\times m$.
Then $AB$ is $m\times m$ and $BA$ is $n\times n$.
Equal matrices must have the same size, so $m=n$.
Hence $A$ and $B$ are both $n\times n$: square and of the same size, so both (a) and (b) hold.
$c_1$ is the entry in row 1, column 1 of $AB$: (row 1 of $A$) $\cdot$ (column 1 of $B$).
Row 1 of $A$ is $(1,2)$ and column 1 of $B$ is $(1,2)^T$.

qs.q: Suppose that $A_{3\times2}$ and $B_{2\times3}$ are two matrices. Which of the following expressions is defined?
e: $AB$: inner dimensions are $2$ and $2$ (equal), so the product is defined and is $3\times3$.
$A+B$ and $A-B$ require equal sizes, but $A$ is $3\times2$ and $B$ is $2\times3$, so they are not defined.
Only $AB$ is defined.

qs.q: Suppose that $A$, $B$ and $C$ are three matrices such that $AB=AC$. Which of the following statements is true?
e: Cancelling $A$ is only allowed when $A^{-1}$ exists: $A^{-1}(AB)=A^{-1}(AC)\Rightarrow B=C$.
The problem does not say $A$ is invertible, so (b) and (c) are not guaranteed.

Counter-example: $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}$, $B=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix}$, $C=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\5&6\end{bmatrix}$ give $AB=AC=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&0\end{bmatrix}$ but $B\neq C$.
Of course $B=C$ also satisfies $AB=AC$, so $B$ may or may not equal $C$.

qs.q: Suppose that $A_{1\times2}$, $B_{2\times3}$ and $C_{3\times2}$ are three matrices. Which of the following expressions is defined?
e: $AB$: $(1\times2)(2\times3)$, inner sizes match, result $1\times3$.
$(AB)C$: $(1\times3)(3\times2)$, inner sizes match, result $1\times2$. So $ABC$ is defined.
$ACB$: $AC$ is $(1\times2)(3\times2)$, inner sizes $2\neq3$, not defined.
$CAB$: $CA$ is $(3\times2)(1\times2)$, inner sizes $2\neq1$, not defined.

qs.q: Suppose that $A_{3\times2}$, $B_{2\times3}$ and $C_{3\times2}$ are three matrices. Which of the following expressions is not defined?
e: $ABC$: $AB$ is $3\times3$, then $(3\times3)(3\times2)$ is defined, giving $3\times2$.
$(A+C)B$: $A$ and $C$ are both $3\times2$, so $A+C$ is $3\times2$; then $(3\times2)(2\times3)$ is defined.
$(A+B)C$: $A$ is $3\times2$ but $B$ is $2\times3$; different sizes, so $A+B$ is not defined.
Therefore (c) is the expression that is not defined.
$3B=\begin{bmatrix}3&0\\6&9\end{bmatrix}$.
$A-3B=\begin{bmatrix}1-3&2-0\\0-6&3-9\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-2&2\\-6&-6\end{bmatrix}$.
$c_2$ is the entry in row 1, column 2, so $c_2=2$.

qs.q: Suppose that $A_{3\times2}$ and $B_{2\times3}$ are two matrices. Which of the following expressions is defined?
e: $AB$ is $(3\times2)(2\times3)=3\times3$, a square matrix, so $(AB)^2=(AB)(AB)$ is defined.
Powers $A^k$ ($k\ge2$) require $A$ to be square. $A$ is $3\times2$, so $A^3$ is not defined, hence $A^3B$ is not defined.
Likewise $B$ is $2\times3$ (not square), so $B^3$ is not defined, hence $AB^3$ is not defined.
